item.title: Some reports from Summer 2026
item.author: diptanuj.ds@gmail.com (Diptanuj Sarkar)
item.dc:creator: [Diptanuj Sarkar]
item.description: I spent the summer at IISER-K, trying to cover the preliminaries for my MS Thesis project at the EPQM group.
item.content:encoded:
This summer, I stayed over on campus to try and do some preliminary readings for my MS Thesis at the EPQM Group.

My supervisor handed me a few things to read, in order:

  1. Condensed Matter Physics - The Very Short Introduction, Ross H. McKenzie (link): A very nice introductory book, goes over the various phenomena that interests condensed matter physicists, and how they approach their study.
  2. Emergent Particles and Gauge Fields in Quantum Matter, Ben J. Powell (link): A review article, goes over the moving parts of the “Standard Model of Materials” (A.K.A. The GLW Paradigm), and then moves on to a description of several quantum matter systems that fall outside of that scaffold. A fair bit more technical than Ross’ book.
  3. Condensed Matter Physics: Does Quantum Mechanics Matter?, Michael E. Fisher (link): On the ocassion of a symposium in the honor of Niels Bohr, Michael Fisher wrote this brief overview of condensed matter physics as it stood then. It was written at an interesting turning point in the history of condensed matter physics - right about the time when Quantum Hall Effects and High-Temperature Cuprate superconductors were taking center stage.
  4. There’s plenty of room in the middle: The unsung revolution of the renormalization group, Nigel Goldenfeld (link): An article that lends support to Fisher’s critical view of quantum mechanics leaking into condensed matter physics, from a more modern perspective.
  5. The Physics of Quantum 2.0: Challenges in understanding quantum matter, Siddhartha Lal and Mayank Shreshtha (link): An article written by my supervisor, which starts off by reviewing that historical stepping-stones in the study of condensed matter, and the questions/challenges that theorists have to face now.

I wrote some reports based on my reading of these sources, which you may find below. They aren’t the best - but atleast they were written by a human :)

You can find them listed below.

Summer is almost over - looking forward to my MS Project!

item.title: Things that are broken
item.author: diptanuj.ds@gmail.com (Diptanuj Sarkar)
item.dc:creator: [Diptanuj Sarkar]
item.description: Short story that I submitted for an inter-batch competition at IISER-K, in 2026. I ended up winning! ( Thanks Tarak! :) )
item.content:encoded:
Before you read the story

This is the first coherent (?) thing that I have written in years, and it is partially the reason why I decided to start putting them up here to begin with. It might be a bit corny, but I tried to write down what I felt like at that point - Writing is a skill like any other, and I will try to improve!

Link to IISERK Literature Club post. (Instagram)

Enjoy 😄

Things that are broken

The unholy odor of freshly wetted garbage wafted down the alley, slightly annoying the man. It was unpleasant. But at least Kolkata hasn’t turned into the goddamned Kalahari yet, he thought.

He walked with a spring in his step, this otherwise disgruntled-looking man. There was a stubble on his face, and an altogether respectful amount of beer in his belly. Just enough to give him a spring in his walk, but not enough to make him stumble. Barely anything could make him stumble, you see. This here was a hard man, a man who fancied that he had seen it all - and liked none of it. Give him lemons, and he would save them for his weekly tequila. He had on one of those waxy-looking jeans one could find for 200 or so at New Market near the end of the day. Above that, a t-shirt that was perhaps brown in color. It might have said something along the lines of “I love NYC” at some point on it, but it had been eroded into only two disjoint splotches of white. Nothing to say, after all. He had never been to New York anyway.

The wet garbage, as you may remember, was wetted by the first rain shower of the year. Cursing the Alipur Weather Department, like the millions of opinionated (and drunk) Bengali men making their way to a roll joint who came before him, the man ducked into a nondescript shop near the middle of the alley.

He had no intention of buying anything; he only wanted to avoid the rain. His cynical self couldn’t help but wonder what inspires someone to set up shop in a place like this. They definitely won’t be getting a lot of traffic. The rest of the alley was shuttered, and a dog seemed to really be enjoying the day.

The front of the shop gave the man pause. A short door, cracked in places due to age, separated the alley from the inside. The cracks were deep, and he spotted a lot of dirt in them. I wonder how long that dirt has been there. There was a small plant, barely clinging onto life with two tiny, minuscule leaves, that had taken root in one of those cracks. Maybe today was its lucky break.

With no windows to peer inside, the man pushed the door open right away. He never had a sense of ceremony.

Inside, it was quite dark. It was old, both in how it looked and how it smelled. A small room, perhaps about the size of the carrom room in his local sporting club. The walls were not grimy, but old cobwebs crusted in dust lined the top corners.

He derived great pleasure from the idea that whoever maintained this shop must be mighty short and must have never heard of a dusting stick. The last comment was particularly enjoyable to him.

The floor was speckled marble tiles, a design truly only appealing to the mid-twentieth-century Bengali. All around him, lit by two or maybe three terrifyingly yellow tungsten bulbs, were tables.

Many sorts of tables - old mahogany tables, cracked linoleum tables, and the disgusting red plastic ones with a hole in the middle. There were many of them, so many that there was barely any way forward!

On these tables, placed with evident care, were myriad things. Really, an absolute myriad. The man, now confused, thought he saw a Rubik’s cube, an old crusty-looking watch, a children’s slate, a bunch of pens of several different types, a dried-up succulent, and wait… is that an empty bottle of Absolut vodka? Intrigued and perhaps a bit scared, though he would never admit it, the man walked towards the table in front of him.

He picked up the dusty Rubik’s cube on it and tried to recall all of those algorithms he learnt in the cubing club at school. Turning it around, he noticed that the center blue tile on the cube was gone - a broken cube is no good.

A thin cough filled the room, and the man dropped the cube right onto the marble floor in shock.

“Ki chai apnar? (What do you want?)” said the severely old man standing in the corner of the room. The man realized that he must have been there the entire time - he must be the owner.

The man hurriedly explained the rain (the old man must be hard of hearing, he thought) and that he had just ducked into the store to spare himself a good drenching.

The old man’s face betrayed no particular emotion. The man found comfort in this - he had always believed that a sane person is almost always a dispassionate one.

The old man was clean-shaven, and wrinkly all over. His hair held the white fluffy nature of a roadkill pigeon.

Greyish pyjamas and a wonderfully colorful shirt were on this person. The kind hippies wore to an orgy, you know.

Faced with the dissonant, incoherent image of the old man before him, the man looked down at his feet and realized that the cube had promptly shattered—another tile missing. He hurriedly picked it up, and as he was about to ask for its price out of shame, the old man spoke in his surprisingly meek voice: “Don’t worry about it. A broken thing only gains in character once it is broken again.”

What a curious thing to say, thought the man. Maybe this guy was an honest-to-god hippie from ye olden days. He had never met one, but always wondered why they were so happy.

“What kind of shop is this - antiques?” asked the man.

“I sell broken things,” replied the old man.

A thousand sarcastic comments flooded our protagonist’s mind as he grappled to rein them in, for the old man may yet let him wait out the rain.

“Fuck Alipur,” he mumbled as he blurted out the obvious next thing to ask. “Why?”

“Because all broken things must have secrets in them,” answered the hippie.

He was getting a bit annoyed, the man, that is. While a curious little shack in the old city with a strange old character in it was an appealing plot device, the dissonance that this drunk and happy man felt emanating from the oldie was a visceral sort of feeling. He swallowed it.

Saying nothing in reply, for fear of engaging the strange man, he picked up the slate. It fell apart into two—the thing wasn’t even glued together. On the back, a small scribble declared a possible past owner, a child. ‘Ratal,’ it said, ‘Section A.’

“Once there was a child, around 5 or 6, in a village in Hooghly. Bright kid, really liked the rumble of chalk on a slate. His brother gave him this slate as a present when he started school. I saw the child break it into two and chuck it into the pond. I think the school closed - some budget act?” the old man recited to the man. The buzzing of alcohol calming down, the man might have just ignored him. But he did see the remnants of a ‘ক’ character on the slate, clearly written down over and over again on the same spot with great care. Perhaps it will never get erased entirely.

Surprising himself, the man reached for the cube again.

“What about this thing?” he asked no one in particular.

“Mukesh, I knew in school. Never interested in anything, the pessimist type. A teacher gave him a cube, that very one, when he scored well on a math test in 5th grade. He had cheated, of course, but he had the cube now nonetheless. Day and night he solved the cube - over and over. Gave him some sort of purpose, I wager. He ended up doing a PhD in something terribly complicated, last I heard. He left it behind in the school desk drawer when his family moved - I took it.”

“People actually buy this shit,” the man could not hold it in anymore. The old man gently smiled at him.

“Not as many as I would like, I am afraid,” he said.

“Secrets are a precious commodity, but people rarely realize this. I would say nowadays, but they never really have,” he continued.

Not understanding a word but feeling like he was in a headspace that had escaped him for a few decades, the man just asked:

“What secret?”

The old man walked towards him and held out his hand for the cube. The man handed it over, and the old man twisted it a few times into a more entropic mix.

“See, it turns well even now. It was one of those magnetic ones, very pricey back then.”

“You see how faded the colors on the tiles are? How scratched the corners are? That boy loved his cube,” he said.

“But what secret! That is not a secret!” the man was taken a bit aback by how interested he felt in this.

“Well, babu, it was a secret to you before. It is not anymore - this secret of Mukesh’s love for his cube. But it remains a secret to everyone else, you see?”

The conviction with which this was said to him was a strange thing to experience. It was true, what the old man said. Perhaps a benign fact in a world full of them, but a fact nonetheless.

He looked at the crusty watch with a dirt-filled embossing of ‘Love, Anjali’ around the dial. He did not ask a question.

The rain had stopped, that much was clear to him. He looked at the old man, who was holding one of those mass-produced metal rickshaw showpieces they sell in Haridwar gift shops. It was missing a wheel. The old man looked content.

“The rain has stopped. Ami elam, dada (I’ll take my leave),” said the man.

As the door opened up and the light outside blinded him for a second, the man, for the first time in a few decades, thought of nothing but the smell of rain and wet garbage.

He turned around, and his eyes descended to meet the poor two-leaf plant on the door. The splashes had taken one of the leaves off.

He bent down and touched the cold, wet, sole surviving leaf with a tenderness that his friends did not know him for.

He smiled.

He wondered why he ever thought that the world was a sphinx without a secret. He told himself that he would remember the leaf. Perhaps, the leaf would remember something of him.

item.title: The Ethics of Belief, William K. Clifford
item.author: diptanuj.ds@gmail.com (Diptanuj Sarkar)
item.dc:creator: Diptanuj Sarkar
item.description: Reading at the Mohanpur Circle. Deals with the question: Is it always wrong to hold a belief without proper justification?
item.content:encoded:
The original text: The Ethics of Belief

Relevant SEP page: Ethics of Belief

11/01/202511/01/202511/01/2025

Brackets are used to express questions that arise in my mind while reading the text.

Clifford relays a story to motivate his claims: A shipowner is going to sell tickets for a transatlantic journey. He gets doubts (they are possibly presented to him, with/without evidence) that the ship is not seaworthy. The shipowner is initially unhappy but does not investigate any further and manages to acquire a “sincere and comfortable conviction” that the vessel is safe. He sells the tickets, the ship sails and then sinks, and he collects the insurance money.

Clifford claims:

  • The shipowner is guilty of the deaths of those on the ship.
  • The shipowner may have been sincerely convinced (note: is this even possible?) of the seaworthiness of the ship, but he is still in the “wrong” (assumed to be a moral wrong) because “he had no right to believe on such evidence as was before him”.

How does Clifford justify this?

  • He had not earned the belief by patient investigation of evidence.
  • He had knowingly worked himself into the state of mind where he believed in the seaworthiness.

Thus, he must be held responsible for the “wrongness” of his belief.

Clifford alters the story, imagining an outcome where the journey is completed safely. He claims that even in this case, the shipowner is in the wrong. Why?

  • Clifford says that action once carried out is either right or wrong forever. No outcome, good or evil, can change that.
  • The shipowner in this case was not right, he just wasn’t found out and saved by sheer accident.

In summary, Clifford believes that it does not matter if a belief turns out to be true or false, but whether the person holding said belief had a right to believe on such evidence as was before them.

Another story: A group of people are professing a religion that goes against some predominant religious notions on some islands. Those not part of this newer religion have a suspicion that those involved with it are using unfair and unethical (?) means to preach to children. In response, a group formed and they published grave accusations against the people involved with the new religion, without investigating their claims. A commission is formed to investigate them, and the accusations are found to be entirely false.

Clifford uses this to make the same claim as in the story before.

He addresses a doubt - we may say that it is not the belief that is in the wrong, but the action following upon it.

  • The shipowner may say, “I am certain that the ship is safe, but it is my duty to have her examined”.
  • The agitators may be told, “You may be convinced of your allegations, but you ought not to have made a public attack without investigating them further”.

Clifford admits that this view is right and necessary,

  • Why right? Even with fixed belief, a person always has a choice regarding any action suggested by the belief. Thus, they have the responsibility to test their convictions.
  • Why necessary? “Those who are not yet capable of controlling their feelings and thoughts must have a plain rule dealing with overt acts”. (What does this mean? Who are the people “not capable” of said control? What “overt act”?)

He points out that the view is not sufficient (clear from the fact that he calls it necessary), and that we require his previous claim (of there being no right to believe on insufficient evidence) to supplement this view. He claims that,

  • It is not possible to sever the belief from the action it suggests. Thus, we can not condemn one without condemning the other.

Why? He reasons that a person who believes in (or, is even inclined towards) one side of an argument/question may never be able to investigate it with the fairness and completeness of someone who has no such bias. (Is it true that our biases are always stronger than our belief in the process of proper investigation?) He goes ahead and makes a stronger claim: A belief that does not have any influence on the actions of the person who holds it is not a true belief. (Then what is a belief that does not inspire action? Say, I have a belief that includes that clause that says if I ever act in a way that lets others know of said belief, I would be committing a wrong deed. Is such a thought not a belief for Clifford, or is he contesting that such a thought simply can not exist?) He claims that,

  • Any person who has ever wanted to commit an action inspired by some belief has “already committed it in his heart”. (How can committing something “in the heart” equivalent in anyway to real action?)
  • If a belief is not immediately causing a real action, it is “stored away” to influence future actions - it goes into some part of our minds, made up of an aggregate of beliefs, that is the link between sensation and action at all moments of our lives (So, are all of our actions motivated by a belief or some remnant of it? Are there no actions not motivated by beliefs?)
    • Further, he claims that this “aggregate” can not be separated into the constituent beliefs, and each new belief inducted into it changes its structure.
  • So, every belief (true belief, as he defines it) is linked to some action, ultimately. Not only that, but each belief opens us up to more similar beliefs.

As a result, Clifford argues that no person may have something akin to a “private belief”. This, combined with the claim that humans live in societies where we have shared, common heritage, leads him to draw the conclusion that any belief (no matter how trivial) has far reaching consequences. So, he extends his judgement to all beliefs held by all sorts of people, and claims that individuals have to earn their beliefs by examination because they hold these beliefs for all of humanity.

He acknowledges that the burden of such thorough examination of ourr beliefs is a heavy one, and reasons that this is not only because of the difficulty in carrying out such examination but also because we feel safe and secure in holding a fixed belief whereas doubting it makes us bare and powerless. This sense of power attached to believing is what makes people desirous of believing, and afraid of doubting. He argues that we should earn said power through our examination of evidence instead of resorting to a fake sense of power - as justified belief enriches not just the individual holding the belief but also mankind as a whole. Additionally, he claims that unjustified belief not only runs the risk (or, in his view the certainty) of wrong action, but it also encourages others to belief without justification. This perpetuates the problems of unjustified belief. On the other hand, a person who seeks evidence for or against his belief inspires a similar spirit of inquiry in others, thereby making mankind more virtuous. Thus, he states his principle - It is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence. He proceeds next to make an every stronger statement, saying that once inquiry has been completed to the greatest extent possible and a belief accepted, it is still the duty of every person holding a belief to continue to be open to evidence for or against the belief. (Is he not ccontradicting himself? If the belief is accepted as justified at some point in time, is the person holding the belief not “biased” as he puts it before - and thereby incapable of a fair assessment of further evidence? So, does belief-acceptance bar a person from belief-relinquishment?) He finishes the section by saying that a person who does not have the time for such inquiry should not have the time to believe.

(Notes incomplete)

item.title: Euler-Lagrange equations: A derivation
item.author: diptanuj.ds@gmail.com (Diptanuj Sarkar)
item.dc:creator: Diptanuj Sarkar
item.description: This is me trying out KaTeX on the site
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

We start off by taking as a prototype the simple Newtonian scheme of a point particle of mass mmm moving along the x-axis under a potential field V(x)V(x)V(x).

According to Newton’s Second Law of motion,

md2xdt2=−dVdx m \frac{d^2 x}{dt^2} = - \frac{dV}{dx} mdt2d2x​=−dxdV​

If we are given the position and the velocity of this particle at some initial time, i.e. x(ti)x(t_i)x(ti​) and x˙(ti)\dot{x}(t_i)x˙(ti​), then it is possible for us to compute the classical trajectory of the particle xcl(t)x_{cl}(t)xcl​(t) as follows

xcl(t+Δt)=x(ti)+x˙(ti)Δt x_{cl}(t+\Delta t) = x(t_i) + \dot{x}(t_i) \Delta t xcl​(t+Δt)=x(ti​)+x˙(ti​)Δt

We can keep following the same iteration scheme to calculate the position at t+2Δtt+2\Delta tt+2Δt, t+3Δtt+3\Delta tt+3Δt, and so on.

Since the equation of motion is second order in time, there are two pieces of data (namely, x(ti)x(t_i)x(ti​) and x˙(ti)\dot{x}(t_i)x˙(ti​)) that are required to specify a unique xcl(t)x_{cl}(t)xcl​(t). An equivalent way to doing the same thing is to specify an initial point (xi,ti)(x_i,t_i)(xi​,ti​) and a final point (xf,tf)(x_f,t_f)(xf​,tf​) (Why?).

In the Lagrangian formalism, the same problem is posed in this way: Given the initial and the final point, what is it that distinguishes the actual classical trajectory joining these point from the infinite other trajectories that join these two points? The answer to this lies in the following points:

  • Define a function L\mathbf{L}L, called the Lagrangian which is given by,

    L=T−V \mathbf{L} = T - V L=T−V

    TTT and VVV being the kinetic and potential energies of the particle. Thus, L=L(x,x˙)\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{L}(x,\dot{x})L=L(x,x˙). Note that we assume the absence of ttt dependence by considering a potential field that is not time-dependent.

  • For each path x(t)x(t)x(t) connecting (xi,ti)(x_i,t_i)(xi​,ti​) and (xf,tf)(x_f,t_f)(xf​,tf​), calculate the action, defined by,

    S[x(t)]=∫titfL(x,x˙)dt S[x(t)] = \int_{t_i}^{t_f} \mathbf{L}(x,\dot{x}) dt S[x(t)]=∫ti​tf​​L(x,x˙)dt

    There are square brackets because we want to remember that the argument of S is the entire path or the entire function x(t)x(t)x(t), not just the value of the function at some time. SSS is thus also called a functional.

  • Principle of Least Action: The classical path is the one on which SSS is a minimum (Actually, it is only required that it be an extremum. The name is merely customary).

Now, we verify whether this principle gives us back Newton’s Second Law.

A multivariable detour

Since SSS is a function of some other function x(t)x(t)x(t), it is really just a multivariable function of nnn variables as n→∞n\rightarrow \inftyn→∞. This is due to the fact that the function x(t)x(t)x(t) actually specifies an infinite number of values x(ti),…,x(t),…,x(tf)x(t_i), \dots , x(t) , \dots , x(t_f)x(ti​),…,x(t),…,x(tf​) - one for each instant in time ttt in the specified interval. We will deal with the entire minimum (actually, extremum) situation of the action by generalising how we deal with it in n variables. Let us define a function,

f=f(x1,…,xn)=f(x⃗) f = f(x_1, \dots , x_n) = f(\vec{x}) f=f(x1​,…,xn​)=f(x)

The minimum of this function, say, x0⃗\vec{x^0}x0 is characterised by the fact that if we move away from it by a small amount η⃗\vec{\eta}η​ in any direction, the first order change in fff vanishes. Using the Taylor expansion,

We now use the property that we deduced to arrive at the extremum of SSS. We assume that xcl(t)x_{cl}(t)xcl​(t) is the path of least action (as per the principle), and that xcl(t)+η(t)x_{cl}(t) + \eta(t)xcl​(t)+η(t) is a “nearby” path. As all the paths have to coincide at the initial and the final points, we get the condition,

η(ti)=η(tf)=0 \eta(t_i) = \eta(t_f) = 0 η(ti​)=η(tf​)=0

So now we get to the main attraction,

S[xcl(t)+η(t)]=∫titfL(xcl(t)+η(t),x˙cl(t)+η˙(t))dt S[x_{cl}(t) + \eta(t)] = \int_{t_i}^{t_f} \mathbf{L} (x_{cl}(t) + \eta(t),\dot{x}_{cl}(t) + \dot{\eta}(t)) dt S[xcl​(t)+η(t)]=∫ti​tf​​L(xcl​(t)+η(t),x˙cl​(t)+η˙​(t))dt

⇒S[xcl(t)+η(t)]=∫titf[L(xcl(t),x˙cl(t))+∂L∂x(t)∣xcl⋅η(t)+∂L∂x˙(t)∣xcl⋅η˙(t)+⋯]dt \Rightarrow S[x_{cl}(t) + \eta(t)] = \int_{t_i}^{t_f} \bigg[ \mathbf{L} ( x_{cl}(t), \dot{x}_{cl}(t) ) + \frac{\partial \mathbf{L}}{\partial x(t)} \bigg \vert _{x _{cl} } \cdot \eta(t) + \frac{\partial \mathbf{L}}{\partial \dot{x}(t)} \bigg \vert _{x _{cl} } \cdot \dot{\eta}(t) + \cdots \bigg] dt ⇒S[xcl​(t)+η(t)]=∫ti​tf​​[L(xcl​(t),x˙cl​(t))+∂x(t)∂L​​xcl​​⋅η(t)+∂x˙(t)∂L​​xcl​​⋅η˙​(t)+⋯]dt⇒S[xcl(t)+η(t)]=S[xcl(t)]+δS(1)+ higher order terms  \Rightarrow S[x_{cl}(t) + \eta(t)] = S[x_{cl}(t)] + \delta S^{(1)} + \text{ higher order terms } ⇒S[xcl​(t)+η(t)]=S[xcl​(t)]+δS(1)+ higher order terms 

Since this is the case with infinite variables, the sum involving the first order partial derivatives of the action has been converted into an integral. Using the fact that we deduced earlier regarding the first order change going to zero, we can say,

0=δS(1)=[∂L∂x(t)∣xcl⋅η(t)+∂L∂x˙(t)∣xcl⋅η˙(t)]dt 0 = \delta S^{(1)} = \bigg[ \frac{\partial \mathbf{L}}{\partial x(t)} \bigg \vert _{x _{cl} } \cdot \eta(t) + \frac{\partial \mathbf{L}}{\partial \dot{x}(t)} \bigg \vert _{x _{cl} } \cdot \dot{\eta}(t) \bigg] dt 0=δS(1)=[∂x(t)∂L​​xcl​​⋅η(t)+∂x˙(t)∂L​​xcl​​⋅η˙​(t)]dt

If we integrate the second term by parts with the partial derivative as the first function and the η˙\dot{\eta}η˙​ term as the second function (Why? It has η˙(t)\dot{\eta}(t)η˙​(t), and we know that η\etaη cancels out at the ends) we get:
